Hrithik's father had shouted again at breakfast, so by the time he reached Class 6 his hands were itching for something to push against. His eyes settled on Tushar, the quiet boy who folded his geometry box shut and never answered back. On Monday Hrithik called him "Snail." On Tuesday he nudged Tushar's elbow so a pencil line ran across the page. On Wednesday Tushar's bag vanished from its hook and turned up on the roof of the cycle stand. Minakshi giggled from the back row, a few others did too, and nobody said stop. Hrithik glanced around, saw the grins, and felt taller than he had all week.

Tushar's stomach began to hurt on Sunday nights. In the mornings he stood at the gate with his palm pressed to his belly. He wondered what was wrong with him that made him the one picked, and he replayed his own walk and his own voice. When Amma asked why he was quiet at dinner, he said, "Just tired," because if she came to school, Hrithik would find out and it might get worse.

qa.q: Where did Tushar's bag end up?
qa.a: It turned up on the roof of the cycle stand.

qa.q: How did Hrithik's first acts and the class's reaction lead to Tushar's secret suffering?
qa.a: Hrithik began small with a nickname, a nudge and a hidden bag, and the grins showed nobody would stop him, so the cruelty seemed to pay. Tushar took it as his own fault and hid it from Amma, and that silence let it continue.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling when the others grinned at the bag on the roof?
qa.a: He felt powerful and admired, taller than he had all week, which fits a boy chasing status after a shouting morning at home.

qa.q: What could Amma do if she notices Tushar's stomach aches on Sunday nights?
qa.a: She could stay calm, tell him it is not his fault, ask gently what happens at school, and speak to the class teacher the same day.

grounding: Shows the first stages of a bullying cycle: a boy picking a quiet classmate, testing with small acts before an audience, and the target's secret shame.

Gautam had made a joke of Anirban's lunch box again, holding up an idli and squeaking like a mouse. Around the mango tree, the others reacted in their own ways. Some winced. A few laughed too loudly, glancing at Gautam. One boy added a joke of his own. Most looked at their shoes, each thinking someone else would speak. Nobody did.

The next day at break, Swati walked over and sat beside Anirban on the low wall. "Come play with us," she said. "We need one more for the game." Anirban hesitated and then went along. After lunch, with her heart thudding, Swati stayed behind at the classroom door. "Ma'am, Gautam keeps mocking Anirban. I didn't want to just watch." The teacher put down her pen. "Thank you for telling me. That was brave, and it was right."

By afternoon the teacher had sat with Anirban and told him this was not his fault, spoken to Gautam alone, and informed the head. Gautam lost his games period. The counsellor asked him what was going on and learned that he was jeered at every evening at home. Gautam was given the job of looking after the sports equipment, and the teacher checked on Anirban each morning that week.

qa.q: What did Swati say when she sat beside Anirban?
qa.a: She said, "Come play with us. We need one more for the game."

qa.q: How did the bystanders' behaviour at the mango tree differ from Swati's, and how did adults later handle both Anirban and Gautam?
qa.a: The bystanders winced, laughed or looked at their shoes, each waiting for someone else to act, while Swati sat with Anirban and then told the teacher. The adults then protected Anirban, gave Gautam a consequence, and had the counsellor find out what was going on at home.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling as she stayed behind at the classroom door?
qa.a: She felt nervous but determined: her heart was thudding, yet she did not want to just watch.

qa.q: Why is telling the teacher not tale-telling in this story?
qa.a: It protected Anirban and changed the mood, and the teacher called it brave and right; staying silent would have left the mocking going on.

grounding: Shows the bystanders' dilemma, an ally who sits with the target and tells a teacher, and adults who protect the target while consequence and support reach the child who bullied.

Preeti held out her hand for a second laddoo. Swati had already given her one after the evening meal. Jeevan, home late and still holding his office bag, shook his head. "No more sweets tonight, sweetheart." Preeti's face crumpled. "I hate you!" she yelled, and stamped so hard her sandal squeaked on the tiles.

Then she tried a new way. She cried in big gulps. "I'll eat all my dinner tomorrow, promise, promise." Jeevan did not answer, and she watched his face from behind her fingers. When that did nothing, she screamed at the top of her voice and threw herself onto the sofa cushions, one eye open to see whether he would move toward the sweet box.

Jeevan's ears burned. Hearing those words after a long day stung more than he expected. His voice was already climbing in his throat, ready to match hers, and he nearly told her she could go to bed without her story. He stopped, set down his bag, and let out a long breath through his nose. Only then did he look at his daughter again.

qa.q: What did Preeti do when she was told no more sweets?
qa.a: She yelled "I hate you!" and stamped so hard her sandal squeaked on the tiles.

qa.q: How did Preeti's tries after the first refusal connect to the moment Jeevan had to handle?
qa.a: Preeti went from shouting to crying, promising and screaming while watching Jeevan's face to see whether he would move toward the sweet box. His ears burned and his voice climbed, so taking a long breath before he looked at his daughter again was the key moment.

qa.q: What might Jeevan be feeling when Preeti yells "I hate you"?
qa.a: He feels stung and tired: his ears burn and his voice is climbing to match hers.

qa.q: What could Jeevan do next, now that he has breathed?
qa.a: He could calmly keep the limit on sweets, tell her he sees she is angry, and stay close for comfort without shouting.

grounding: Shows an early caregiver-child tantrum sequence: a refused sweet, bargaining and testing of the limit, and the parent's own trigger and pause.

Darshan had snapped "Enough!" once, and it only made the wailing louder. Now he crouched to Preeti's height. "I can see you're very angry," he said. "There won't be any more sweets today, though." He did not raise his voice again, and he did not bargain or lecture. He stayed close, hands open, while Preeti wailed and kicked at the rug.

The storm ran down slowly. Preeti hiccupped, sniffed, and after a minute crawled into his lap and pressed her wet face into his shirt, half ashamed and half relieved. "I said a mean thing," she whispered. "You did, and I still love you when you're angry," Darshan said. He rubbed her back until her breathing evened out.

At bedtime, with Leela's plates clinking in the kitchen, they talked about it. "What could you do next time your anger gets big?" Preeti thought. "Stomp softly. Draw it. Or ask for a hug." "All good ideas," Darshan said. "And I'm sorry my voice got loud earlier. I'm working on that too." Preeti considered this seriously, then asked whether they could draw an angry monster together.

qa.q: What ideas did Preeti give for handling anger next time?
qa.a: She said to stomp softly, draw it, or ask for a hug.

qa.q: How did Darshan's calm limit lead to Preeti climbing into his lap, and what did the bedtime talk add?
qa.a: By staying calm and close without shouting or bargaining, Darshan let Preeti's storm run down, so she felt ashamed and relieved and came for comfort. At bedtime they planned other ways to handle anger, and his apology showed that people can make things right.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling when she crawled into his lap?
qa.a: She felt half ashamed and half relieved, and seemed to need to know her angry words had not broken things between them.

qa.q: What did Darshan's apology at bedtime teach Preeti?
qa.a: It taught her that even a parent can raise a voice and then repair it, which makes fixing things feel possible for her too.

grounding: Shows the later caregiver-child stages: a calm firm limit, the child's return for comfort after the storm, and reflection with skill building and a parent's apology.

During the lesson on cells, Usha asked why the slide showed only one kind of stain, and Mr. Asif paused. It was the third careful question she had asked that month. After class he held out a slim paperback on how scientists work. "Read it if you like. No test on it." Usha carried it home as if it were made of glass. Nobody outside her family had ever picked something out just for her.

Two weeks later she lingered by his desk until the corridor emptied. "Sir, I want to be a doctor, but I'm not sure I'm clever enough." She braced for a laugh or a pat-on-the-head answer. He only asked, "What makes you think that?" and listened to the long reply, then said the marks she described were not the whole story. Her shoulders loosened.

By the end of term, Reena groaned that Usha started every argument with "Let's look at the evidence first," exactly as Sir did. Usha repeated his views on textbooks, on cricket, on which subjects were serious, as though they had come from a stone tablet.

qa.q: What did Mr. Asif hand Usha after the lesson on cells?
qa.a: He handed her a slim paperback on how scientists work.

qa.q: How did Usha's guarded visit to his desk lead to her copying his phrases?
qa.a: Usha lingered by his desk, braced for a laugh, and asked whether she was clever enough to be a doctor. His listening replies lowered her guard, and later she started every argument with his phrase and repeated his views as if they came from a stone tablet.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling as she braced for a laugh at his desk?
qa.a: She felt nervous and exposed, worried that her doubts about becoming a doctor would be laughed off.

qa.q: What could Usha do to keep admiring Mr. Asif while still using her own judgement?
qa.a: She could weigh his views against evidence and other opinions, as he would probably encourage, and notice where she sees things differently.

grounding: Shows the early mentor arc: a teacher noticing a student's questions, the student's cautious openness at his desk, and admiration that starts to copy his words.

passage:
Mr. Jatin's comments on her project were blunt: the question was vague, two graphs had no labels, and the conclusion claimed more than the data showed. Pallavi's ears burned. She wanted to crumple the report and say something rude. That evening she read the margin again and noticed he had also written the three steps that would fix it and, at the bottom, "You can do better than this, and I say so because I know it." She redid the graphs that night.

Months on, she picked biology instead of the engineering-heavy stream he had recommended, and dreaded telling him. Her voice shook. Mr. Jatin took a moment. "I would have picked another one. Still, tell me how you got there, because I'd like to hear it." They talked as two people now, and she left the room taller.

He kept the rules simple: they met in the open lab or at the open-hour slot with the door wide, and he copied her form teacher on the emails. Once he added, "If any adult ever asks you to keep chats or gifts secret, tell your mother straight away." At home Pallavi repeated it to her mother, Dilnaz, who nodded and said she would like to meet the teacher at the science fair.

qa.q: Which stream did Pallavi choose?
qa.a: She chose biology instead of the engineering-heavy stream Mr. Jatin had recommended.

qa.q: How do Mr. Jatin's blunt comments and his reaction to her stream choice show the bond changing?
qa.a: The margin notes were blunt and made her ears burn, but he wrote the steps to fix the graphs and said she could do better, so she redid them. Months later she picked biology instead of his stream, her voice shook, and he listened to her reasons, so they talked as two people.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling when she told him about her stream choice?
qa.a: She felt nervous and afraid of his disappointment; her voice shook.

qa.q: Why does Mr. Jatin meet in the open lab and copy the form teacher on emails?
qa.a: It keeps the relationship professional with others aware, so the guidance stays safe, and he adds that any adult asking for secrecy should be told to a parent.

grounding: Shows the later mentor arc: blunt but caring critique, the student's independent choice against advice, and safe professional boundaries.
